title: Stopping for sweetness
what: For a white Lot: ferment dry, or stop the yeast partway at about 15, 35 or 60 g/L of sugar by chilling the tank and adding SO₂.

steps: Sugar left in the wine with any live yeast
can start fermenting again in the bottle
so the wine must be sterile-filtered, or it turns spritzy and hazy

choose: It suits high-acid Riesling. Kabinett needs 73 °Oe and may not be chaptalised, so the sugar you keep is the grapes' own. Each 16.8 g/L kept is about 1 % vol less alcohol. Acidity offsets sweetness: EU label terms raise the dry and medium-dry limits for high-acid wines.
exam: Expect 'how is sweetness kept in German Riesling?'. Name this method and what it leaves (sugar, lower alcohol), why it suits a high-acid grape; sweet reserve (unfermented juice added before bottling) is the other route, though not for top-quality Kabinett.

check.question: Your 80 °Oe Riesling (about 183 g/L of sugar) should end light, about 9 % vol, with clear sweetness. Which plan?
options: Stop at about 35 g/L by chilling and SO₂, then sterile-filter
Ferment dry: the acidity will read as sweetness
Stop at about 15 g/L and skip sterile filtration
Chaptalise first so more sugar is left
check.answer: Stop at about 35 g/L by chilling and SO₂, then sterile-filter
check.why: Fermenting 148 of 183 g/L gives about 8.8 % vol and keeps 35 g/L of sweetness; any sugar left needs sterile filtration, and a Prädikat wine may not be chaptalised.

simplification: Game simplification: the Lot stops exactly at the chosen sugar level; a real, fast-fermenting tank overshoots by a few g/L while it cools.
